mappings.note: Both contain the superscription: 'To the choirmaster. Of Asaph. On the Gittith.' (Norwegian: Til korlederen. På Gittit. Av Asaf / French: Au maître-chantre. Psaume d'Asaph, sur Guitthith).
Both contain the call to sing with joy to God and Jacob's God.
Both list the instruments: tambourine, lyre, harp.
Both mention blowing the horn at new moon, full moon, and the feast day.
Both state this is a law/ordinance for Israel/Jacob's God.
Both describe the statute for Joseph and the voice heard in an unknown language upon leaving Egypt.
Both describe God lifting the burden from the shoulder and hands releasing the basket.
Both contain the cry in distress, deliverance, answer in thunder, testing at Meribah, and the Selah marker.
Both contain 'Hear, my people' and the conditional 'if you would listen to me'.
Both forbid foreign gods. (French: 'ne te prosterne pas devant les dieux des nations' vs Norwegian: 'du skal ikke tilbe en utlendings gud'). The meaning is identical.
Both identify God as the one who brought them from Egypt and promise to fill an open mouth.
Both state that the people did not listen/would not have God.
Both describe letting them go according to their own stubborn hearts/plans.
Both express the wish that the people would listen and walk in God's ways.
Both describe subduing enemies and turning against adversaries.

The translation splits the content of OSMAIN v16 into two separate verses (v16 and v17). OSMAIN v16 contains both the punishment clause ('hater... underkaste seg') AND the promise clause ('give them wheat/honey'). The French version separates these into v16 (punishment) and v17 (promise).
This verse contains the second half of OSMAIN v16 ('God would have fed them...'). It is not an extra verse in terms of content, but a split of the source text.
